headline: Peconic pushes into the mid-70s — porgies thick at Shelter Island, bass slide onto the night shift
subhead: A softening neap tide this week means slower presentations and bonus fish for anglers willing to fish the edges of daylight.
body_markdown:
The Peconic runs its own calendar, and right now it's deep into the part of the summer where the bay stops being a nursery and starts being a feeding ground. Surface temps have pushed into the mid-70s across most of the system — warmer in the back coves off Noyack and Three Mile Harbor, a touch cooler out toward Orient where the tide from Gardiners Bay keeps flushing it clean. That gradient is doing exactly what it does every July: pulling porgies tight to structure, keeping fluke locked on the channel edges, and pushing the striped bass into a low-light pattern that's frustrating anybody who only fishes banker's hours.

Start with the porgies, because right now they're the most dependable thing happening in this bay. Shelter Island is holding them thick — Majors Harbor, the flats off Cedar Point, and the drop-off outside Jennys Creek are all loaded with scup in the 20 to 35 foot range. High-low rigs with size 6 or 8 hooks, tipped with sandworm or a piece of clam, fished right on bottom on the last two hours of the incoming through the top of the tide. That's when the current is strong enough to hold the chum slick together but not so ripping you're re-anchoring every twenty minutes. Anybody complaining about porgy fishing this week either isn't using fresh bait or isn't looking at a tide chart — this bite doesn't require much finesse, just the right window.

Fluke are the other constant. We said last week this bite would carry through the summer, and it has — the channels between North Haven and Shelter Island, the cut off Jockey Creek, and the deeper stretch of Noyack Bay are all holding fish. Nothing gigantic, but a steady grade of 16 to 19 inch fluke with the occasional four or five pounder mixed in, especially on the last of the ebb when bait gets pulled off the flats into the deeper water. Three-quarter ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet or a squid strip, dragged slow along the bottom in 15 to 25 feet, is still the go-to. Drift with the tide, not against it — these fish are sitting in the current seams waiting for food to come to them, not chasing.

Stripers are where things get more honest. The warm surface water has done what it always does this time of year — pushed the better class of bass into a nocturnal or dawn/dusk pattern. Daytime fishing in the open bay has been slow and I won't pretend otherwise. But Plum Gut and the rip off Orient Point are still producing after dark and in that gray light right before sunrise, when the current is really moving through the Gut on the ebb. Eels and bunker chunks fished on the bottom, or swimbaits worked through the rip on a slow retrieve, have been taking slot fish and the occasional overslot. Jessup's Neck and the drop-off along Nassau Point are worth a shot at first light too — smaller fish, mostly schoolies and low-slot, but they'll eat a white or bone Slug-Go worked over the grass edges before the sun gets high.

Weakfish are starting to show some life again, which lines up with what we expected — calm, warm evenings have a way of waking this bite back up. Noyack Bay and the cove off Sag Harbor have both given up a few weakfish in that 3 to 5 pound range on quiet nights, mostly on bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow just off bottom. It's not a bite you can plan a whole trip around yet, but if you're already out there for stripers or fluke at dusk, it's worth a few extra casts along the drop-offs.

Bluefish have been chopping through bunker pods scattered around the bay, particularly off Southold and out toward Orient, and they're a nice bonus for anyone fishing light tackle with kids aboard — poppers or diamond jigs will get bit fast when you find the birds working.

The tide is the story to watch this week. We're sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which means the current through Plum Gut, the Race, and the connecting cuts around Shelter Island is going to soften noticeably over the next several days. That's not bad news — it's an opportunity. Slower current means you can slow your presentations down too, which tends to produce better quality on both fluke and any blackfish sniffing around structure right now. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take advantage of that softer water to work the deeper holes around Shelter Island with a slower bucktail drift, then swing over to Plum Gut right at last light while the tide's still got enough push to hold bass on the rip.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change dramatically — the porgy bite should hold strong through August, the fluke should stay steady as long as the channels keep their bait, and the bass will keep favoring darkness until the water starts cooling down in September. Keep an eye out toward Orient and the mouth of the bay for early false albacore or bonito scouting activity as the month wears on — the water's warm enough now that it wouldn't surprise me to hear the first reports any week.
